circuits.description: The five-knob Deluxe version of the Lunar Module: the same three-transistor silicon fuzz with the pregain trim brought out as a Range control, a Body control setting the bass into the fuzz section, and a Brite control in place of the filter trim.

circuits.name: Soulsonic FX Hunny Bunny
circuits.description: Martin C.'s (Soulsonic) original overdrive, a hybrid of op-amp and discrete styles: an LM301 non-inverting stage with Tube Screamer-like frequency shaping drives a BS170 MOSFET that does the overdriving. The 'Honey' pot sets how much the MOSFET's source is bypassed, from tight 'British' crunch to thick saturated distortion.

circuits.name: Tone Monk Seed of Life
circuits.description: Gutshots showed the Seed of Life to be a Tube Screamer built on a General Guitar Gadgets ITS8 PCB, populated as GGG's 'Expensive Boutique Screamer' mod, which is the same circuit as the Landgraff Dynamic Overdrive. It uses a TL072, symmetrical silicon-diode clipping with two red LEDs on the board, a slightly skewed tone control and a 'fat' toggle switch.
notes: The post's advice: to build one, buy a GGG ITS8 PCB and use the Expensive Boutique Screamer values.

circuits.name: Top Tone Light Drive (Pete Cornish SS-2)
circuits.description: The Top Tone Light Drive, a straight clone of Pete Cornish's discontinued SS-2, traced by MWichini on freestompboxes. A 741 non-inverting gain stage with a 50k Drive pot feeds a pair of 1N270 germanium diodes to ground, a passive tone control and a second 741 stage before the Volume pot. The post notes it lacks the Cornish input buffer: add the buffer schematic in front of it to get an SS-2.
notes: Run the Cornish input buffer (the second schematic in the post) in front of this circuit to make a full SS-2.

circuits.name: Pete Cornish Input Buffer
circuits.description: Pete Cornish's high-impedance, unity-gain class A input buffer, which sits at the input of his pedals: a single BC549 emitter follower with a bootstrapped bias network and a 10M input resistor. The post gives it so it can be put in front of the Light Drive to make a full SS-2.

circuits.name: Univox Super-Fuzz
circuits.description: The Shin-ei designed Super-Fuzz made by Unicord for Univox from 1968 into the late 1970s, used by Pete Townshend among many others. A two-transistor input gain stage feeds a phase splitter driving a long-tailed pair, whose shared collector gives full-wave rectification and the upper octave, then a pair of germanium diodes clip it. A tone switch engages a mid-scooping filter around 1 kHz, and a final transistor stage drives the output. The post quotes mictester: high-gain transistors for the first two and a matched long-tailed pair give more octave; silicon clipping diodes make the biggest change.
notes: mictester: the circuit works best with high hFE transistors for the first two (he used BC109C) and lower gain for the rest; almost any silicon transistor works.
Matching the long-tailed pair transistors and the resistors around them gives much more octave.
Swapping the germanium clipping diodes for silicon gives the biggest change in sound.

circuits.name: Ibanez Standard Wah Fuzz (fuzz section)
circuits.description: The fuzz section of the Ibanez Standard Wah Fuzz, a close relative of the Super-Fuzz. A 2SK30A JFET input stage replaces the Super-Fuzz's two-transistor input, then the same phase splitter, long-tailed pair octave rectifier, germanium diode clipping, switched tone filter and output transistor follow.

circuits.name: Boss FZ-2 Hyper Fuzz
circuits.description: Boss's Hyper Fuzz, a later descendant of the Super-Fuzz. A JFET input buffer feeds a differential gain stage with the Gain pot, then a Super-Fuzz style phase splitter and long-tailed pair with diode clipping. Op-amp filter stages, a three-way Mode switch (boost, fuzz I, fuzz II), active High and Low EQ and Boss's JFET electronic switching with a flip-flop finish it.

circuits.name: Wampler Pinnacle Distortion (Limited Edition)
circuits.description: Wampler's 'Brown Sound' distortion: two cascaded J201 micro-amp stages with bootstrapped gate bias (the dual micro booster developed from the Brown Sound in a Box II DIY circuit), a J201 buffer, a passive tone and contour network, and a TL072 make-up gain stage. A footswitched Boost turns on MPF102s that switch extra source bypass into each gain stage.
notes: No layout yet; the post suggests adapting a BSIAB II layout.

circuits.name: Wampler Pinnacle II
circuits.description: A schematic said to be the Pinnacle II: the same pair of bootstrapped JFET micro-amp stages with a DPDT boost switch adding source resistors, a JFET buffer and tone/contour network, but with a JFET output stage in place of the op amp.

circuits.name: ZVEX Woolly Mammoth
circuits.description: The ZVEX Woolly Mammoth, a bass fuzz designed by Chuck Zwicky that also works on guitar and draws under half a milliamp. The post describes it as the standard Fuzz Face layout with mods: large coupling caps that pass deep bass, a Big Muff style tilt EQ at the output and a Pinch control that sets the feedback between the two silicon gain stages, changing the pulse width and adding a gating effect.

circuits.name: Dallas Rangemaster
circuits.description: The 1960s germanium treble booster: a single PNP germanium transistor (OC44 or OC71) in common emitter, with a small 0.005uF input capacitor that sets the treble emphasis. Used to push dark British valve amps by Clapton, Brian May, Iommi, Blackmore and Gibbons. The post stresses precision metal film resistors and a well-regulated supply, since the circuit is prone to hiss.
notes: Tuning (from R.G. Keen's Geofex article): temporarily replace the 68K (Rb1) with a 100K pot and the 3K9 (Re) with a 10K pot, adjust for -6.6 to -7.2V on the collector with a fresh battery, then fit the nearest standard values; if Rb1 ends up below 27K or above 82K, or Re below 2.7K or above 5.1K, use another transistor.

The input capacitor (nominally 5n) may need to be as much as 6.8n for some transistors; smaller thins the sound, larger boosts lower notes, and around 150n boosts all notes for a full-range soft distortion that is not the original sound. Stay within about +/-50% of 5n for the original voice.

circuits.name: D*A*M Red Rooster
circuits.description: D*A*M's updated Rangemaster: a single NPN germanium transistor booster with a Range control that sweeps from treble boost through full range to bass boost, and a trimmer to set the bias. The post builds it from a vero layout copied from the D*A*M board.
notes: Set the trimmer for about 6.66V on the transistor collector.
Use an NPN germanium transistor with an hFE of about 100; higher hFE gives more grit.

circuits.name: D*A*M Ezekiel 25:17
circuits.description: David Main's bass distortion for D*A*M: a non-inverting op-amp buffer, then an op-amp diode clipper whose 470R/10uF ground leg amplifies the full bass range (unlike a Tube Screamer's 720 Hz high-pass), a passive filter control and a blend with the clean signal. A four-position rotary switch selects the clipping diodes, from germanium and silicon pairs to LEDs.
notes: The vero suggests a JRC4562D op-amp, or a JRC4558 or similar.
The rotary switch is a single-pole, four-throw (a 4-position 3-pole switch with one pole used).

circuits.name: Fred Briggs Unknown Fuzz
circuits.description: The blog author's own silicon fuzz, grown out of experiments with the Vox Tone Bender. The first stage is a pair of piggy-backed high-gain 2N5088s trimmed to an hFE of about 25 to act like a low-gain germanium device, driving a NOS BC108 second stage. There is no gain control; the guitar's volume knob takes it from mild overdrive to full fuzz, and the author describes it as fat and warm rather than harsh.
notes: Add a 2n2 cap in parallel with the 22K resistor and the Width pot to calm the high end and upper mids; the author used it in his final build.
Piggy-backed transistors are picky; you may have to try several pairs of 2N5088 before one works well.

circuits.name: Fulltone PlimSoul
circuits.description: Fulltone's PlimSoul combines soft and hard clipping. The first op-amp stage is a standard overdrive with asymmetric silicon diode clipping in its feedback loop; the second stage's Stage 2 control is a dual-gang pot that raises that stage's gain while lowering the resistance in series with a pair of red LEDs clipping to Vcc/2, so the LEDs glow with the distortion. A Hi-Cut, Level and a C1815 output buffer follow.

circuits.name: Tim Escobedo Bazz Fuss (rev 1.5)
circuits.description: Tim Escobedo's final version of Hemmo P.'s Bazz Fuss: a single Darlington (one MPSA13 or two 2N3904) with diodes from collector to base, here one 1N4148 one way and three diodes the other for more volume and smoother clipping. A 10k rheostat on the emitter sets the gain from fairly tame to fuzz. An optional input transformer (primary winding only) preserves the circuit's tone when it follows a buffered effect or active pickups. The post calls it a DIY classic to tweak freely.
notes: The input transformer (Mouser 42TM018, primary only: 10k impedance, 550 ohm DC resistance) can be omitted when the pedal is driven directly from a guitar with passive pickups.
Two 2N3904 in a Darlington pair can replace the MPSA13; other Darlingtons will probably work.
The post suggests tweaking the diodes and the input and output capacitors.

circuits.name: RunOffGroove Bazz Fuss v3
circuits.description: The minimal Bazz Fuss as hosted by Home-wrecker: one MPSA13 Darlington with a 10k collector resistor and a single diode from collector to base, followed by a 100k audio volume pot. The clipping diode is the part to experiment with, as the post's comparison chart shows.
notes: Diode comparison (Home-wrecker): 1N34A, 0.22V: decent, but output is too low. 1N914, 0.57V: the stock version, great fuzz. 1N34A plus 1N914, 0.78V: a bit more defined and louder. Two 1N34A plus 1N914, 1.0V: almost a hybrid fuzz/distortion. Orange LED, 1.8V: a hybrid distortion/overdrive.

circuits.name: Jen (Gretsch Playboy) Harmon Booster
circuits.description: A vintage Jen-made booster sold as the Gretsch Playboy Harmon Booster: a chain of silicon NPN stages, several of them buffers, with a Big Muff style tone control between two emitter followers before the volume. Nightraven describes it as an overdrive that borders on fuzz with the controls dimed, which he prefers to Tube Screamers.

circuits.name: Mictester Silicon Tonebender
circuits.description: Mictester's consistent silicon fuzz: four BC109C transistors, a Tone Bender-style core with a 47K feedback/bias resistor, followed by an emitter follower and a tone control. The Abuse pot sets the gain, Sparkle has a very wide treble range, and a Fat/Thin switch picks the input cap. Mictester likens the sound to early Jeff Beck.
notes: Setup: set the Abuse pot halfway, play through it, and adjust the 5K trimmer until the gating just stops.
Add small caps from base to collector of the middle two transistors (start with 47p) to smooth the sound, at the cost of treble.
For radio interference, add 100p from the base of the first transistor to ground.
The 8.2n tone cap (C7) can go as low as 3.3n for a much wider treble range.
Raise the 47K feedback/bias resistor (R8) as high as 470K for more gain: touch sensitivity disappears and it becomes a high-gain screaming fuzz.
The vero layout notes the input cap can be anything from 10n to 10u, to taste.

circuits.name: Gus Smalley Hot Silicon
circuits.description: Gus Smalley's 2003 silicon Tone Bender with tone control, a silicon version of Aron Nelson's Hot Fuzz, shown in the post as a near twin of the Mictester design: four 2N5089s, a 47K feedback resistor, an emitter follower and a tone control, with a Fat switch on the input cap.
notes: R9 can be replaced with a 5K trimmer and tuned to taste.
S1 gives the fat tone when on; use a toggle or a pot with a pull switch for a 'pull fat' control.

circuits.name: Nine Volt Nirvana BrontoBoost v3.0
circuits.description: Joe Gagan's widely variable boost, fuzz and distortion: a PNP silicon emitter-follower buffer into a dual-gang tone network, a 2N3906 gain stage and a germanium 2SB54 stage, with a clipping diode pair before the volume. A 3PDT switch selects single-stage mode, where it can sound close to a Rangemaster; the post calls it a favorite of gain freaks.

circuits.name: Nine Volt Nirvana Dino Drive
circuits.description: An overdrive and distortion built around a Fuzz Face core (2N3906 silicon into a 2SB54 germanium transistor), followed by a dual-gang tone control and a 2N3906 recovery stage. An SPDT channel switch brings in a rhythm volume with a high-pass cap. The drawing notes it cleans up with picking dynamics and guitar volume.
notes: Set the bias with the 25K trim to -4.5V for smooth distortion, or -6.0V for full low end on the cleaner settings.
Tune the 500K trim to accentuate high end at the full clockwise sweep of the tone pot.
The 1u cap across the drive section is optional, for 'plexi' voicing.
Try different values for the .001uF high-pass cap on the rhythm volume.

circuits.name: Nine Volt Nirvana Dinosaur Fuzz
circuits.description: The earlier relative of the Dino Drive: a pregain pot and simple tone control into a 2N3906 and B22 germanium Fuzz Face pair, with an SPDT channel switch for a rhythm volume and a 2N3906 output stage. This is the version from Aron Nelson's site.
notes: Bias: set the trim for -4.5V at Q2's collector.
Turn the treble trim fully counterclockwise, and clockwise to taste for accentuated highs.
Install a socket for the .001uF cap at the rhythm volume for easy modding.

circuits.name: Nine Volt Nirvana Easy Face
circuits.description: A simple hybrid Fuzz Face: a silicon 2N3906 for Q1 and a germanium PNP for Q2, with a pregain pot at the input in place of the usual fuzz control. The post says the silicon/germanium pairing set the foundation for many later boutique fuzzes.
notes: Q1 can be a PN2907, NTE159 or similar; Q2 any good germanium PNP (AC128, NKT275, 2SB173).
Set the bias with the 10K trim to -4.5V between Q2's collector and ground, or by ear so the sound cleans up with the guitar volume a little below half.
Socket Q1 and Q2 and try several germaniums.

circuits.name: Nine Volt Nirvana GT Fuzz
circuits.description: Another Fuzz Face hybrid, designed for Gary Tamas, with much more tone control: a dual-gang 'Fat' control that also feeds gain-stage feedback to Q2's base, a dual-gang tone control, and a third 2N3906 gain stage to restore bite. The pregain is a switched pot that bypasses itself.
notes: Set the control to 'fat' and tune the 10K trim until the squeal stops.
Definition is tuned by the .005uF cap (drawing calls it C2); try values from .1 to .005.
The optional 10K resistor reduces treble bite when the guitar volume is lowered.
Use a hot germanium transistor for Q2 and bias it to -4.5V with the 20K trim.

circuits.name: Nine Volt Nirvana Nitroburner Fuzz
circuits.description: A Fuzz Face variant with a 'Fuel' pregain and tone control, a panel bias pot, and an automotive voltmeter on the front panel that reads Q2's collector voltage in test mode through a 2N3906 meter driver.
notes: Set the bias with the test switch off: turn the 5K bias pot to minimum, then set the 10K trim for -4.2V on Q2's collector.
Use a high-gain germanium transistor for Q2.

circuits.name: Nine Volt Nirvana Skyripper Fuzz '07
circuits.description: Joe Gagan's wild, highly interactive fuzz: a buffer stage, a germanium 2N2614 treble booster, then a Fuzz Face-style 2N3906/2N2614 pair, with a germanium diode 'ripper' feedback path and an expression loop. It gates, octaves, oscillates and stutters; the author built it before the Zvex Fuzz Factory schematic was public and likes it as much.
notes: Q2 and Q4 can be any non-leaky PNP germanium (2SB172, AC128); suggested gains Q2 90-100, Q4 125-175. Q3 any medium-gain PNP silicon.
Biasing, collector to ground: Q2 -6.8 to -7.1V; Q4 -4.5 to -5.3V with S4 closed, -1V with S4 open.
Use a Switchcraft 12A jack for the expression loop return so the loop is closed when unused.
S1 bypass, S2 treble boost bypass, S3 cutboost, S4 rip bias.

circuits.name: Nine Volt Nirvana Tape Measure Boost
circuits.original: Nine Volt Nirvana Tape Measure Boost
circuits.description: A single-transistor 2N2222 clean boost with collector-to-base feedback bias and an output level trimmer.
notes: Transistor substitutes: 2N5088, BC108, ECG123, 2N3904.

circuits.name: Nine Volt Nirvana Tarpit Meltdown
circuits.description: A heavily tweaked Fuzz Face (2N3906 silicon and B22 germanium) with a 2N3906 output stage, plus diode clipping and feedback 'Melt' and 'Hot' controls that push it into meltdown territory. An optional sag pot on the supply is drawn.
notes: Set the bias with the 25K trim for -4.5V at Q2's collector.
The 50K sag control is optional.
Experiment with different types of diodes.

circuits.name: Nine Volt Nirvana Tone Dog
circuits.description: A cut-down BrontoBoost: a 2N3906 emitter-follower buffer and tone network feeding a single 2SB54 germanium stage, with a gain pot, a clipping diode pair and a tone trimmer at the output.
notes: A jumper (stock) or a resistor (10K, 33K, 100K) in the socket by the .0047uF cap reduces highs.
Install a cap (1.0uF, .08uF, .047uF) in the socket at the tone trimmer for a tone control; leave it empty for full frequency response and gain.

circuits.name: Sola Sound Tone Bender MKI
circuits.description: The first British fuzz, Gary Hurst's take on the Maestro FZ-1: three PNP germanium transistors on a -9V supply, with an emitter follower into two gain stages. The Attack pot sets the bias of Q2. The post calls it the most temperamental circuit the author has built, and points to the Geofex Zonk Machine article for biasing tips.
notes: Sinner's turret layout uses a 180K bias resistor on Q2; the post says most builders use 470K there, and the layout itself recommends 470K for better bias.

circuits.name: Gary Hurst Tone Bender MKI
circuits.description: Gary Hurst's own build of the Tone Bender MKI, the same three-transistor germanium circuit as the Sola Sound unit with a few extra parts: a 2.2K/33K divider around the Attack pot, an electrolytic coupling cap between Q2 and Q3, and a 56K load after the output cap. The post says RnFR's vero can build either version by leaving out the Hurst parts.

circuits.name: Hornby Skewes Zonk Machine
circuits.description: The Zonk Machine, made in Leeds in 1965-66, is a near copy of the Tone Bender MKI: three germanium PNP transistors with an emitter-follower input, smaller input and output caps and a few resistor changes. This drawing adds a 1M input pulldown and an LED.

circuits.name: Hornby Skewes Zonk Machine (Jonaz version)
circuits.description: Another Zonk Machine version, traced from an original unit pointed out by Jonaz. Same three-transistor germanium structure as the Tone Bender MKI, with a 33K resistor under the Fuzz pot divider and a 47n output cap.
notes: The tracer measured gains of 70, 116 and 97 for Q1-Q3 and suggests socketing the transistors.
The Zonk is very bright: try input caps between 1n and 10n, perhaps on a three-way switch.
Use a log/audio-taper Fuzz pot; a linear one limits the useful range. It mostly sets the bias of Q2.
An SPST switch across the 2.2M output resistor gives a much louder, nastier sound.

circuits.name: Hornby Skewes Zonk Machine (alternate version)
circuits.description: A trace of yet another original Zonk Machine. Compared with the Jonaz version it has a 220K bias resistor, a 25K Fuzz pot, a 1.8M output resistor and OC71 transistors in the second and third stages.

circuits.name: D*A*M FZ-673
circuits.description: A small custom run by D*A*M of a modified Zonk Machine circuit, adding an input cap blend (the Filter control) to the three-transistor germanium fuzz. The post has no schematic, only Sinner's layout.

circuits.name: Sola Sound Tone Bender MK1.5
circuits.description: Sola Sound's 1966 two-transistor Tone Bender, built around a pair of Mullard OC75 germanium PNP transistors on a positive-ground supply. Its circuit is the same as the Arbiter Fuzz Face that followed later that year, and Vox used it with a few value changes for their Italian Tone Bender. It is less saturated than the three-transistor MKI.
notes: The usual Fuzz Face gains suit it: about 80-90 hFE for Q1 and 110-130 hFE for Q2.

circuits.name: Sola Sound / Vox Tone Bender MKIII (3 knob)
circuits.description: The last of the classic Tone Benders (1968), sold as Sola Sound, Vox and Colorsound units. A three-transistor germanium PNP fuzz with a different structure from the MKI and MKII: a directly coupled Q1/Q2 pair feeds a Fuzz pot and germanium diode into Q3, followed by a passive Treble/Bass blend. The post describes it as more mellow and less aggressive than the earlier Tone Benders, though still capable of a lot of fuzz.
notes: In the original the transistors were unmarked PNP germanium and the diode a 1N270.
The post recommends a lower gain pair (hFE 40-60) for Q1 and Q2 and a higher gain transistor (hFE 90-120) for Q3.
Electric Warrior's vero layout uses a 250K Volume pot and differs slightly from the schematic (e.g. 50uF and 10uF electrolytics, a 150K resistor and a 1M resistor at the pots).

circuits.name: General Guitar Gadgets Boutique Bender (Fulltone Soul Bender)
circuits.description: Fulltone's Soul Bender is based on the Colorsound and Vox Series III Tone Benders, with three gain-matched germanium transistors and a reworked, less shrill Tone control. The post gives GGG's Boutique Bender vero layout of it, with a bias trimmer.

circuits.name: Tanabe.tv Zenkudo
circuits.description: The post calls it a straight Hermida Zendrive clone using a JRC4558 in place of the AD712, with a three-way diode select switch (MOSFET-and-germanium 'Dumble', 'Zenkudo' and red LED 'Marshall') that also changes a multicolor LED. It quotes PaulC on the odd 10n input cap and 2M2 resistors, which together with the 470n/470K make a small low-end roll-off around 41 Hz.

circuits.name: Tim Escobedo Tytewadd Fuzz
circuits.description: One of Tim Escobedo's circuit snippets: a single bipolar transistor gain stage whose collector load is a J201 JFET acting as a current regulator, which raises the gain enough for big fuzz tones, with a pair of silicon diodes in the feedback. It draws under 10uA from a 9V battery. The post compares it to his Syrupp booster and recommends it for Big Muff-ish tones.
notes: The 220k input resistor can be swapped for a pot for some gain control.
Q1 can be any medium to high gain transistor.

circuits.name: Tim Escobedo SyRuPP
circuits.description: Tim Escobedo's take on the Mini Booster: two J201 JFETs stacked, the top one as a current source with a 100k trimmer and the bottom one as the gain stage with a 2M gain pot, running on 3V from two AA batteries at about 25uA. Fairly clean at minimum gain and pleasantly 'syrupy' at maximum; he uses it as an overdrive.
notes: Can run on 3V to 9V; 3V from two AA batteries and the 22k source resistor are what make it stand out.
Set the 100k trimmer to the sweet spot; several different JFETs all worked.

circuits.name: ToadWorks Mr. Squishy Compressor
circuits.description: A tuned variation of Dan Armstrong's Orange Squeezer: a JFET shunt attenuator ahead of an op-amp gain stage, with the output rectified to drive the JFET, plus a second JFET and Squish pot to set its bias. There is no buffer; the post notes the input can be overloaded so the attenuation JFET clips, and with Squish off it works as a clean boost.

circuits.name: Dan Armstrong Orange Squeezer
circuits.description: The original op-amp and JFET compressor that the Mr. Squishy is based on: a JFET shunts the signal to ground ahead of an op-amp gain stage, and the rectified output turns the JFET on harder as the signal grows. The post shows it for comparison and says it gives transparent compression with quick attack and release.

circuits.name: Dallas Rangemaster
circuits.description: The 1960s Dallas Rangemaster treble booster: one germanium PNP transistor (OC44 or OC71) in common emitter with a small input cap, built to push a tube amp into saturation. Shown as the first of the vintage boosters the post surveys.

circuits.name: Apollo Treble Booster
circuits.description: A vintage single-transistor germanium booster (2SB175) with a 500K Treble/Bass pot that blends between a small 1800pF coupling cap and a larger 22nF path, so it can boost treble or the full range.

circuits.name: Hornby Skewes Selectatone T.B.2
circuits.description: Hornby Skewes' Selectatone treble and bass booster: a single OC71 germanium stage followed by a switch that chooses a 1nF treble path or a 10k/1k/100nF bass path to the output.

circuits.name: Hornby Skewes Treble Booster
circuits.description: Hornby Skewes' fixed-gain germanium treble booster, a single 2N4061 stage with no controls; the same circuit is the treble booster half of the Hornby Skewes Shatterbox. The post notes it was also built with an OC44.
notes: R5 (100k) is not present on all units; it may be replaced with a 100k pot (the assumed Blackmore modification).
Also built with an OC44 germanium transistor.

circuits.name: Orange / Vox / Apollo Treble/Bass Booster
circuits.description: The treble/bass booster sold under the Orange, Vox and Apollo names: a 2SB175 germanium stage with a 500K pot blending a 1800pF treble cap against a 30k and two 0.22uF bass network at the input.

circuits.name: Pete Moore Rangepig
circuits.description: Pete Moore's hybrid Rangemaster: a low-gain germanium OC44 in Darlington with a silicon 2N4402, with a 100k trimmer between them that dials in how much germanium grit the circuit has. The author prefers it to the silicon Rangepig for its tweakability.
notes: MartyMart built it with an OC44 and a 2N3906 and used 47n input and output caps for a more full-range boost.

circuits.name: Will Firstbrook Range Pig Treble Boost
circuits.description: Will Firstbrook's low-noise, negative-ground silicon treble booster that emulates a Rangemaster with piggybacked 2N5210 transistors to mimic germanium's low gain and nonlinearity. Q2's collector is biased to 7V for asymmetric clipping, and C6/C7 cut highs to simulate germanium's high-frequency weakness.
notes: C1 can be increased to 100n for a full-bodied boost.

circuits.name: Fred Briggs Rangemaster
circuits.description: The author's own Rangemaster (2012), using Pete Moore's germanium/silicon Darlington pair (a ~50 hFE germanium Q1 and a ~250 hFE silicon Q2) with a few common Rangemaster mods. It runs from -9V with a polarity diode.
notes: Bias Q2's collector to -6.6V using the 10K trimmer.

circuits.name: Vox Tone Bender
circuits.description: The Italian-made Vox Tone Bender of 1966-68: a two-transistor germanium PNP fuzz with a 47K feedback resistor from the Attack pot to the first transistor's base, in the Fuzz Face family. The quoted review describes it as a raspy, treble-heavy fuzz, between a Rangemaster and a Fuzz Face, with a little less fuzz than an early Fuzz Face.
notes: The 1M input pull-down resistor and the 47uF supply capacitor (drawn in blue) are optional improvements, not part of the original.

circuits.name: D*A*M 1966
circuits.description: D*A*M's discontinued replica of the 1966-68 Vox Tone Bender, with gain-selected germanium transistors (an AC125, OC75 or SFT353 then an OC76) and a two-position switch between the original '66 voicing and a fuller Super Bee voicing. Built here from a stripboard layout by beedotman for turretboard.org.
notes: The 2.2nF capacitor mounted under the board can be omitted if the 4700pF capacitor is increased to 6800pF.

circuits.name: D*A*M Super Bee SB-66
circuits.description: A D*A*M variation of the Vox Tone Bender circuit with larger input and output capacitors for a bolder fuzz. Built here from beedotman's stripboard layout for turretboard.org, positive ground.
notes: Pick transistor gains: beedotman suggests starting with 60-75 hFE for Q1 and 75-105 hFE for Q2, with Q2's collector biased around -6V.

circuits.name: WEM (Watkins) Project V Fuzz
circuits.description: A rare vintage British fuzz from WEM in a very long case, owned by Graham of the D*A*M forum, who ranks it beside the Buzzaround. The circuit is unusual: an input pair with a small HF inductor in the first transistor's emitter feeds the Attack pot, then a multi-transistor gain and output section with low-value emitter resistors, while the Drive and Edge slide switches reconfigure filtering and feedback around the input and output.
notes: The 470p capacitor can be 390p and the two 4.7 ohm resistors can be 5.1 ohm (alternatives on the drawing).
The Q7 and Q8 BC108B positions (and Q6) can use BC109B.
The layout notes say the inductor is optional and can be replaced with a jumper, or with a TDK EL0606 series or similar of under 10 ohms.
The layout adds an optional 220p capacitor (its C17) that tames the fuzz's harshness, silver mica recommended.

circuits.name: WEM / Rush Pep Box (germanium version)
circuits.description: The early germanium Pep Box, a 1960s British fuzz sold under the Rush and WEM/Watkins names and used by John Lennon around the Revolver era. Two PNP ACY41 germanium transistors run from -9V, the Effect pot sitting between them as both the interstage level and the second transistor's base bias. A 3300pF output cap thins the low end before the Level control.

circuits.name: WEM / Rush Pep Box (silicon version)
circuits.description: The later WEM Pep Box with NPN BC107 silicon transistors on +9V. The circuit follows the germanium version, with a 1M base resistor and a 10n cap from the first base to ground, and a trimmer of unknown value where the germanium version has its 820K resistor.

circuits.name: Dean Markley Overlord Tube Overdrive
circuits.description: A 12AX7 tube overdrive with an internal mains transformer, a close relative of the B K Butler Tube Driver: a 4558 input buffer and drive stage feed the two triodes, followed by a passive Hi/Bass/Mid tone stack. The author owns one and plans to mod it toward the reissue Tube Driver (true bypass, the Bias control replacing Mid, an external 16VAC supply with regulation, Tube Driver values).
notes: The author's planned mods: true bypass; replace the Mid control with the Tube Driver's Bias control; remove the internal transformer and run from a 16VAC adapter with a regulated supply like the Baja Real Tube Overdrive; change the stock values to match the reissue B K Butler Tube Driver; shielded wire for off-board signal runs.

circuits.name: B K Butler Tube Driver (early garage-made version)
circuits.description: The original B K Butler Tube Driver: a 4558 buffer and gain stage drive both halves of a 12AX7 in cascade, then a Hi/Lo tone stack and output level. Powered from a 24VAC center-tapped transformer with split +13V/-14V rails and a 16V heater/LED rail. The author shows it as the core design behind the Overlord.
notes: The tracer's notes on the drawing: R7 and R8 would be expected to be 47K (the unit may have been modded for lower-gain tubes such as 12AT7/12AU7); C2 should be non-polarized, a film cap where possible; the main difference from the newer version is R14, which goes from 2.2K to 22K.
V1 can be a 12AX7, 12AT7 or 12AU7 per the drawing. The drawing suggests rewiring for true bypass.

circuits.name: Tube Works Real Tube RT-901
circuits.description: B K Butler's Tube Works version of the Tube Driver: a TL072 buffer and gain stage into a cascaded 12AX7, then a Hi/Lo/Mid tone stack. It adds a TL072 flip-flop driving J112 JFET switches for soft-touch bypass, with red/green status LEDs.

circuits.name: Tube Works Blue Tube RT-903
circuits.description: The Tube Works Blue Tube, the same board and switching as the Real Tube with a 100K series resistor before the first grid and 220K/47K in place of the 10K/10K bias divider on the second triode, plus a handwritten 100K Hi pot. A Tube Driver variant the author compared when planning his Overlord mod.

circuits.name: Tube Works 303 Smooth
circuits.description: A later Tube Works pedal on the RT-901/903 board: TL072 input buffer and gain stage ('Push') into a cascaded 12AX7, with the tone stack relabeled Ice, Warm and Neutral, J112 soft switching driven by a TL072 flip-flop and status LEDs.

circuits.name: B K Butler Tube Driver Rev 2 (with Bias)
circuits.description: The newer B K Butler Tube Driver with the Bias control, a 10K pot on the 12AX7 cathodes that sets the tube's current and so its gain, texture and dynamics. TL072 buffer and gain stage, cascaded triodes, Hi/Lo tone stack. The author takes its values and the Bias mod for his Overlord rebuild.
notes: Per B K Butler, most players find the Bias sweet spot around 2:30 to 3 o'clock.

circuits.name: Bajaman Real Tube Overdrive
circuits.description: Bajaman's take on the Tube Driver: TL082 buffer and gain stage into a cascaded 12AX7, with the tone stack reduced to a single Tone control and a 7815/7915 regulated split supply from a 16VAC adapter, which the author borrows for his Overlord mod.

circuits.name: Fred Briggs Rangemaster MKII
circuits.description: The author's own Rangemaster variant: a low-gain germanium and a medium-gain silicon transistor in a Darlington pair, building on Pete Moore's RangePig. A Filter control slides from treble boost to full range, an Aggression control blends the germanium tone with the harder silicon sound, and a bias trimmer sets the transistor voltages. Covers everything from a stock Rangemaster to an almost Fuzz Face-like boost.

circuits.name: Skreddy P19
circuits.description: Marc Ahlfs' (Skreddy) Big Muff variant tuned for the lead tones of Pink Floyd's The Wall. He started from the Cornish P1 without its input buffer, then used smaller input caps for articulation and less hum, carbon composition resistors, some ceramic caps and a 0.33uF cap between the tone stack and the output stage to loosen the lows. It is a four-BC550 Muff with a Mids switch on the tone stack.
notes: The clipping diodes are unmarked on the schematic: Marc keeps a slightly asymmetric 'Skreddy recipe' secret; the gutshot looks like 1N4148 types, and the post suggests a slightly mismatched pair of 1N4148s.
It can be built on nearly any Big Muff layout with the right part substitutions.

circuits.name: Soulsonic Folk Driver
circuits.description: A low-gain two-transistor (2N5089) overdrive/boost designed by Soulsonic (MC, 2009) after Bjorn Juhl sent him a BJFe Honey Bee, as a DIY work-alike of its sound. R8 adds positive feedback to raise the first stage's gain, R9 and C4 add negative feedback that smooths the highs, and a 1N4001 plus 1N4148 diode combination clips after the output. The single Timbre control sets both the low end and the drive, with minimum drive at noon, combining the Honey Bee's Gain and Nature controls; the post calls it a subtle enhancer that suits stacking.

circuits.name: Bearfoot FX Pale Green Compressor
circuits.description: The Bearfoot FX Pale Green Compressor, an exact replica of the BJFe Pale Green: a light, transparent optical compressor. A 5534 op-amp gain stage has an LDR in its feedback loop; a transistor envelope follower driving the LDR's LED sets the gain reduction. A dual-gang Tone pot adjusts the EQ both before and after compression. The post says it is a simplification of the Mad Professor Forest Green Compressor, and the schematic is modified from Whitekeyhole's Forest Green trace.
notes: With the Comp knob at minimum it works as a booster/enhancer/EQ.
The Tone control's zero point is at noon: turning left gives a classic Dyna/Ross EQ, turning right adds treble and sparkle.
Runs on 8 to 18V.

circuits.name: Catalinbread WIIO
circuits.description: Catalinbread's Hiwatt-in-a-box: three cascaded BS170 MOSFET gain stages with a tone stack between the second and third, in the same family as the Zvex Box of Rock. Negative feedback from the third stage back to the first (200K and 470n) tames the gain, and the MOSFETs are biased off center by a 62K/100K divider for asymmetrical, tube-like clipping.
notes: The author suggests replacing the 200K feedback resistor (R11) with a B500K pot, and trying other values for the 470n feedback cap (C8): smaller keeps more highs.

circuits.name: Catalinbread RAH
circuits.description: The Catalinbread RAH (Royal Albert Hall) is roughly the WIIO circuit, three cascaded BS170 stages with feedback from the last stage, retuned and given a three-knob Bass/Mid/Treble stack taken from the Hiwatt DR input preamp used by Jimmy Page. Very uncompressed, with a wide dynamic range.

circuits.name: Maxon / Ibanez Super Tube Screamer ST-9
circuits.description: A rare 9 Series Tube Screamer with a Mid Boost (Bite) control placed ahead of the clipping stage; the schematic was made available by Dirk Hendrik. The post recommends it to anyone who likes Tube Screamer type overdrives.

circuits.name: Ibanez STL Super Tube
circuits.description: The STL Super Tube, a later spin-off of the ST-9 that is often confused with it. Electronically it is almost the same Tube Screamer with a mid boost, except that the Bite (mid boost) control comes after the clipping stage rather than before it. It uses the usual JFET switching and flip-flop electronic bypass.

circuits.name: Maxon OD-820 Overdrive Pro
circuits.description: Maxon's 'Klon killer': a 2SK246 JFET input buffer feeds a dual-gang Drive pot that both sets the gain of a 4558 clipping stage (diodes in its feedback loop) and blends between that and a clean path, followed by a mixing stage, a Tube Screamer-style tone control and a volume buffer. A MAX1044 charge pump gives the op-amps +/-9V for extra headroom. The post finds it more transparent than the Klon Centaur, without its mid-range texture.
notes: The parts list gives no part numbers for the clipping diodes; the post suggests 1N914/1N4148 as in most Maxon overdrives, though other diodes work.

circuits.name: Diamond Compressor
circuits.description: An optical compressor built around a VTL5C3 vactrol, with emitter-follower buffers that have current sources in their emitters, an OP275 audio path, an LM358 side chain with double rectification, and a post-compressor 'tilt' EQ taken from an early-1970s Quad stereo preamp that pivots around 900Hz. A bicolor LED shows the depth of compression. The post notes that the current-source buffers and paralleled caps are not really needed for guitar.
notes: The tilt EQ bypass resistors R13 and R14 are not needed and can be removed without an audible difference.

circuits.name: Fred Briggs Diamanté
circuits.description: The blog author's simplification of the Diamond Compressor: the same vactrol opto compressor and LM358 side chain, with the buffers removed or simplified and the tilt EQ left out, leaving only Comp and Volume controls.

circuits.name: Fred Briggs Pharmacy Fuzz
circuits.description: The blog author's own Fuzz Face-type design, with each of the two transistors replaced by a Darlington pair made of a germanium device (about 50 hFE, low leakage) driving a silicon device (about 250 hFE), and a variable resistor between them to set each pair's gain. An Aggression control in the feedback loop acts as an overall gain control, and a Bass Cut control is the familiar Fuzz Face input tone blend. Ferrite beads on the input and a suppression choke in the supply reduce noise and radio interference.
notes: Use a 100k trimmer for the first pair's gain (T1) and a 100k pot for the second pair's gain (T2), since the second pair is where most of the clipping happens.
For simplicity the first Darlington pair can be replaced by a single low- or medium-gain transistor.
Set the 10k bias trimmer for about half the supply voltage (4.5-6V) on the second pair's collector, or wherever it sounds best.
Without the parts, replace the suppression choke with a 100 ohm resistor and leave out the ferrite beads.

circuits.name: Boss DS-2 Turbo Distortion
circuits.description: The Boss factory schematic of the DS-2 Turbo Distortion, part of a look at John Frusciante's Californication-era pedalboard. The post describes it as a complicated design built from discrete op-amp stages with a switchable boost and mid-peaking filter (the Turbo mode). Since no project files existed for it, the author suggests building a Marshall Shredmaster instead.

circuits.name: Boss CE-1 Chorus Ensemble
circuits.description: The Roland/Boss CE-1 Chorus Ensemble factory schematic (ET-10D board), shown for reference: a mains-powered MN3002 bucket-brigade chorus and vibrato with a two-transistor preamp, an op-amp LFO and a peak-level LED meter. The post notes its low input impedance (it was designed for keyboards), its mains power and its size make it awkward on a guitar board, and recommends building the later Boss CE-2 instead.
notes: The drawing's own note: with a uPC1458 for IC-4, R80 must be 120K and R81 150K; with a CA1458G, R80 may be 120K or 180K and R81 160K or 220K.

circuits.name: Ibanez WH-10 Wah
circuits.description: The Ibanez WH-10 factory schematic (Hoshino Gakki, 1993). Unlike a Cry Baby it is inductorless: a dual op-amp state-variable style band-pass filter swept by the treadle pot, with a Gtr/Bass range switch, a JFET switching circuit and a separate tuner output buffer. The post says the treadle pot is a standard linear 50K and points to Dirk Hendrik's project file laid out for a Crybaby shell.
notes: The treadle pot (VR1) is a standard linear 50K (B50K).

circuits.name: Jordan Vico Vibe
circuits.description: The Jordan Vico Vibe, a late-1960s plug-in tremolo housed in the same style of box as the Jordan Bosstone; despite its name it is a tremolo, not a vibe. A 2N5088 phase-shift oscillator drives a second 2N5088 that shunts the signal to ground as a variable resistor, giving a smooth sine-wave tremolo, and also the volume drop the original is known for. Mahoney later made a replica with an added boost.
notes: The 1M trimmer sets the bias of the first (shunt) transistor.
Renegadarian's vero layout adds optional parts: R9 1M, C5 100u and D2 1N4001 for polarity protection.

circuits.name: Lovepedal Silicon Fuzzmaster
circuits.description: A silicon Fuzz Face variant using 2N3906 PNP transistors wired to run from a standard negative-ground supply. The Blend control sets how much signal passes through a 1u cap beside the 4.7n input cap, controlling the bass and fatness, and the Drive network is slightly altered from the stock Fuzz Face. A 10K trimmer in Q2's collector sets the bias.
notes: rmrosa measured the original: the 10K trimmer was set to 2.73K; Q1 pins 1/2/3 at 1.46V, 6.62V, 7.24V and Q2 at 6.62V, 7.48V, 7.93V.

circuits.name: Pigtronix Philosopher's Tone (Germanium Gold)
circuits.description: An optical compressor/sustainer: a VTL5C6 vactrol in the feedback loop of an NE5532 stage, driven by a rectified side chain, sets the gain. Grit blends a diode-clipped (germanium, LED and silicon diodes) version of the compressed signal with a clean one, Blend mixes the dry signal against the compressed/clipped signal, and Treble is a simple treble cut. Runs on internal +9V and +15V rails from an 18V supply.

circuits.name: Rothwell Love Squeeze
circuits.description: A British hand-built compressor designed from scratch rather than around an OTA. A TL072 gain stage has a JFET (2N5457) in its feedback network acting as a voltage-controlled resistor, driven by a rectified and smoothed sample of the output, with two LEDs in the feedback as soft limiters. The post compares its subtle, transparent, non-pumping compression to the Orange Squeezer and calls it a 'tone tidier'.

circuits.name: Arsenio Novo Tube Sound Overdrive
circuits.description: Arsenio Novo's 1995 newsgroup design: a complementary 2N3904/2N3906 pair with all their terminals overlapped, biased by equal resistors in each leg, with a large cap from the emitter leg to ground. The negative feedback around both base-emitter junctions gives a gradual, square-law, tube-like clipping rich in second harmonic. The post finds it COT-like but more natural, with low-to-medium gain blues tones that clean up with the guitar's volume knob.
notes: Novo: adjust the bias trimmer for symmetrical clipping on a scope, or by ear for the most sensitivity around mid-turn.
Novo: drive the input from a low-impedance stage if the guitar has no preamp; do not make the input cap much larger or the circuit cuts out.
Novo: the emitter capacitor can range from 0.1u to 1u for different bass characteristics.
Author's mod: a B100K pot wired as a variable resistor in series after the input cap smooths the tone and reduces gain and harsh highs (or a fixed 10-15K resistor).
Author's mod: raise the input cap to 22n or 33n, depending on how much bass is wanted.
Author's mod: a 4.7n cap in parallel with an A500K volume pot tames the top end.
Author's mod: replace the emitter bypass cap with 470n and add a 10u cap in series with an A4.7K pot in parallel with it, as a gain / low-end saturation control from treble boost to full-range boost.

circuits.name: Fred Briggs P.A.F. Overdrive
circuits.description: The blog author's expansion of the Tube Sound OD: an LF353 input buffer fixes the low input impedance, a Bass control around the input cap, a Gain pot in the emitter bypass, a Treble control, and a second op-amp stage with red LED clipping and a Boost control, ahead of the volume.
notes: The author used a 50K bias trimmer in his build in place of the 20K.
Simplified build: replace the 2.2n cap with 33n in series with 33K, drop the Bass control, bypass the Gain control for full gain, leaving Boost, Treble and Volume (Boost can be an internal trimmer).
The Big Muff-style tone control from the BSIABII (as in the ZVex Box of Rock) also works in place of the Treble control, with the Bass control left out.

circuits.name: Wampler Tweed '57
circuits.description: A JFET amp-in-a-box inspired by mid-to-late-1950s tweed Fender amps, the follow-up to Wampler's Black '65. A J201 input stage feeds a paralleled-J201 gain stage, a Fender style Treble/Bass/Mids tone stack, a second paralleled-J201 recovery stage and a J201 output buffer. An Input Simulator switch picks Normal, Bright or Linked inputs, emulating the jumpered channels of a tweed amp.

circuits.name: Blackout Effectors Mantra Overdrive
circuits.description: An amp-like overdrive with cascaded gain stages: two 2N7000 MOSFET stages (each with a 9V zener from drain to gate) followed by two J201 JFET stages, with a Baxandall-style bass and treble tone stack between the JFETs. The post notes that the higher 10k source resistor on the J201 brightens it compared with the usual Tubes-to-JFETs designs, and that the Baxandall stack is a plus over a simple treble cut.
notes: The post suggests a mod: an option to run only the MOSFET section or only the JFET section for lower-gain tones.
The drawing notes that C1 was moved after C24 for better RF rejection.

circuits.name: Blackout Effectors Fix'd Fuzz
circuits.description: Four stages in a row, each with its own bypass toggle: an LPB-1 style transistor boost, a Hemmo's Bazz Fuss single-transistor fuzz (Fuzz 1), an oddly biased Fuzz Face style two-transistor fuzz (Fuzz 2), and a Big Muff tone stack with a gain-recovery transistor. It is one half of the Blackout Twosome dual fuzz. The regular Fix'd Fuzz has only Boost, Tone and Volume on the outside with the other pots as internal trimmers; the Deluxe (used in the Twosome) puts every control on the panel.
notes: Each of the four stages (Boost, Fuzz 1, Fuzz 2, Tone) has its own bypass toggle.
On the regular Fix'd Fuzz only Boost, Tone and Volume are external; Fuzz 1 and Fuzz 2 are internal trimmers. The Fix'd Fuzz Deluxe has all controls on the enclosure.

circuits.name: Blackout Effectors Musket Fuzz
circuits.description: A modified Big Muff: a 2N5089 booster with a Pre control ahead of the usual two diode-clipping stages, a Big Muff tone stack with a Mids control, and a recovery stage. The Focus control works as a bass blend that sets how much low end reaches the clipping stages; the author likes this, as cutting bass before clipping improves clarity. It is the other half of the Blackout Twosome.

circuits.name: Catalinbread CB30
circuits.description: Catalinbread's take on a 30-watt British amp (an AC30): two 2N5457 mu-amp stages with the Gain pot between them, a Vox style Treble/Bass tone stack where turning up both scoops the mids, and a 2N5457 source-follower output. It is built like the Dirty Little Secret and Formula No. 5; C6 and R2 form a feedback path that lowers the gain at high frequencies, and the 470p C7 strongly limits the low end leaving the first stage.
notes: For more gain: reduce R1 (to about 10K), increase C4 (47n or more), increase C7 (1n to 10n), remove or reduce R7, or make Q5 a JFET gain stage instead of a buffer. These change the frequency response somewhat.
Running the circuit at 18V instead of 9V opens up headroom and adds a little gain; do not exceed 25V, the limit of the 2N5457.

circuits.name: Shin-ei Uni-Vibe
circuits.description: The classic Uni-Vibe: a four-stage phase shifter built from discrete transistor stages, with mismatched phase-shift capacitors and four LDRs lit by an incandescent lamp. Its phase-shift-oscillator LFO gives a skewed, asymmetric sine wave and the famous throbbing pulse. The post points to the Forum Vibe and NeoVibe projects as ways to build a close replica.
notes: The post recommends the Forum Vibe 'Mods' version (easier to tune in) or the NeoVibe as a close replica of the original.

circuits.name: John Hollis Easy Vibe
circuits.description: John Hollis's simplified Uni-Vibe: the four phase-shift stages are op-amp all-pass filters with the Uni-Vibe's mismatched capacitors, driven by LED/LDR opto-couplers from an op-amp triangle LFO instead of a lamp. The post recommends it to less experienced builders as far easier to build and tune than a real Uni-Vibe, with a somewhat different tone.
notes: The opto-couplers are a 3mm low-current LED and an LDR sealed together in heat shrink.

circuits.name: MXR Phase 45 with JC Maillet's Vibe mods
circuits.description: The two-stage MXR Phase 45 with JC Maillet's mods to make it more Uni-Vibe-like: switchable Uni-Vibe-style 10:1 phase-shift cap pairs, a Rate LED, an external Bias control, a faster speed range and a Mix pot for a pitch-shifting vibrato mode. The post notes that small-box 'Vibes such as the Lovepedal Magicboy Vibe are based on the Phase 45. The 2N5458 JFETs must be matched.
notes: [1] A switch selects Uni-Vibe 10:1 ratio cap pairs in the two phase stages.
[2] LED rate indicator (2.4K and LED).
[3] External Bias control (100K pot between two 47k resistors).
[4] Two 8k2 resistors in parallel (4.1K) in series with the Speed pot.
[5] Mix pot for a phaser / pitch-shifting vibrato mode.

circuits.name: Fairfield Circuitry Barbershop Overdrive
circuits.description: Guillaume Fairfield's original low-to-medium gain overdrive/boost: two cascaded J201 gain stages followed by a 2N2222 emitter follower. The Sag control is a 10K pot in series with the supply that lowers the voltage reaching the circuit, changing the compression and coloring of the drive. A VP3203 MOSFET with a 15V zener provides polarity protection. The author finds it transparent and touch-sensitive, great for stacking with other dirt pedals.
notes: Guillaume sets the JFET bias at about 2/3 of the supply (around 6V at each drain); the author suggests replacing the drain resistors R5 and R7 with 25K trimmers to set this more easily.

circuits.name: HipKitty Oxblood Distortion
circuits.description: Meant to make a big amp sound like a boosted Vox AC15: an emitter-follower buffer, then a silicon Fuzz Face pair (2N5088s) with a treble-cut control on the end. The small coupling caps cut the bass, which gives the boxy, small-amp tone.
notes: Use the 10K trimmer to bias the Fuzz Face stage; anything from about 4V to 7V on Q3's collector sounds decent.

circuits.name: ISP Decimator Noise Reduction
circuits.description: ISP's Decimator, a noise reduction pedal that uses a THAT 2181 VCA as a downward expander, steered by an envelope detector with ISP's 'Time Vector Processing' release, which reacts fast to staccato notes and slowly on long sustained ones. The post presents it as a transparent alternative to a classic noise gate, without the tone suck and note cut-off. Reverse engineered from an original on DIYStompboxes.com; Joao Galego drew the schematic and a PCB layout.

circuits.name: Joao Galego Decimator G-String work-alike
circuits.description: Joao Galego's work-alike of ISP's Decimator G-String: the same Decimator VCA and detector, but the guitar feeds the detector directly through an input buffer while the VCA sits in a separate send/return loop, so the noise reduction can be placed after overdrives or a preamp and still track the clean guitar signal.

circuits.name: Mad Professor Snow White Auto Wah
circuits.description: Bjorn Juhl's (BJF) envelope filter for Mad Professor. A 2N5457 JFET input buffer feeds an NE5517/LM13700 state-variable filter, while an LM324 gain stage, rectifier and BC550 current source make the envelope follower that sweeps the filter. The post summarizes My7of9's explanation of the circuit blocks from GuitarPCB.
notes: My7of9's mod: a 1N34 germanium diode for D6 and a 1uF electrolytic for C8 make it funkier.
Raising R18 to 47K lets the Sensitivity pot sit nearer 12 o'clock (gain is the Sensitivity pot divided by R18); keeping R18 at 20K and using a 47K pot does the same.
A side-chain mod lets fuzz or distortion go before the auto wah, with a buffer/splitter and an extra jack.

circuits.name: Runoffgroove Thor
circuits.description: Runoffgroove's Thor emulates a Marshall 100W Super Lead preamp with their Fetzer Valve technique: two common-source JFET stages biased to clip like tube stages, then a JFET mu-amp that mimics the odd-order harmonics of a push-pull power amp. It keeps the small Bright cap of the JTM and early Super Leads and the later 470k/470pF filter before the second stage. A TL071 stage at the end adds the Bottom switch, a bass boost that mimics a 4x12 cabinet's resonance.

circuits.name: Tycobrahe Octavia
circuits.description: The Tycobrahe Octavia, said to have been traced by a Tycobrahe employee from one of Roger Mayer's hand-made Octavias brought in for repair. A high-gain three-transistor fuzz drives a small center-tapped audio transformer and a pair of germanium diodes that rectify the signal into the octave-up. The post calls it an evil-sounding fuzz with swells and bloom, heard on Hendrix's Purple Haze and Band of Gypsys tracks.
notes: To cancel the octave-up effect, switch one of the two germanium diodes out of the circuit.

The vero layout by Dr Tony Balls is an NPN negative-ground version (2N5087 for Q1, 2N4401 for Q2 and Q3, 42TM002 transformer), unlike the PNP positive-ground original, so it can share a daisy-chain supply.

circuits.name: Vox Clyde McCoy Wah
circuits.description: The first wah pedal, made by Thomas Organ/Vox in 1967 from the midrange voicing circuit of the Vox Super Beatle amp. The circuit is the same two-transistor inductor wah as the later Cry Baby, but with low-gain BC109B transistors instead of MPSA18 Darlingtons, which the post says gives a rounder bass response, a 100k ICAR taper pot that puts more quack at the toe end, a Halo inductor and several different component values.
notes: The post points out the original's 'tropical fish' capacitors, which many believe contribute to its character, and recommends a replica Halo inductor (e.g. from arteffect in Israel).
The vero layout uses a 100K linear pot for the wah pot and 220nF for the 0.22uF capacitors.

circuits.name: Dunlop Jimi Hendrix Wah Special JH-1s (Rev. C)
circuits.description: The Dunlop Jimi Hendrix Wah Special JH-1s, shown in the post for comparison with the Clyde McCoy; the post notes it is the same as a standard Cry Baby. It is the classic two-transistor inductor wah with MPSA18 Darlington transistors and a 470K pot.

circuits.name: Wampler Ecstasy / Euphoria Overdrive
circuits.description: Wampler's Ecstasy, later renamed the Euphoria, a Dumble-flavored overdrive. The post calls it a Tube Screamer / Voodoo Labs Overdrive hybrid: an op-amp gain stage whose Bass control is a pot to a big cap in the ground leg (the same bass control as PaulC's Timmy), a three-way switch choosing feedback diodes, diodes to 4.5V, or no diodes (op-amp clipping), then a second gain stage and a variable low-pass treble control. Brian Wampler described the design himself on freestompboxes.
notes: The schematic is a simulation screen grab: the three separate 4.5V voltage dividers (R7/R11, R12/R13, R14/R15) can be replaced by a single divider feeding every 4.5V point.

circuits.name: Bearfoot / BJFe Baby Pink Booster
circuits.description: Bjorn Juhl's buffer and clean boost, the same buffer and boost that sit inside the BJFe 'Deluxe' drives, giving up to about 15dB. It is a single 2N5952 JFET stage: in bypass it runs as a unity-gain buffer, and when engaged the footswitch grounds the Boost pot's wiper so the source bypass sets the gain. It runs from 8 to 18V for more headroom.
notes: Select the JFET for about 4.5V on the drain (or one you like the sound of).
Run it from 18V for extra gain and headroom.

circuits.name: Vemuram Jan Ray
circuits.description: The Vemuram Jan Ray, a Japanese boutique overdrive in a brass enclosure, traced by mmolteratx. It is a Paul Cochrane Timmy in structure: a dual op-amp with a pre-gain bass control, diode clipping in the feedback loop and a passive treble cut before a recovery stage. The only real difference is the treble control's range (it rolls off from about 2.8kHz at maximum, where the Timmy's does at 10.6kHz) and an internal trimmer that varies the effective value of R4, which sets the stage's gain.
notes: Per mmolteratx: use the Timmy's treble control in a different range and you have a Jan Ray.
